title: How To Ask Your Students For The Moon . . . And Get It d-get-it/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin opens with a personal anecdote: a former sixth-grade student reconnects with him decades later and reminisces fondly about a demanding, high-expectation classroom filled with hard work, creative projects, and playful traditions. The former student recalls the hard work, the challenging routines, and the neverending calls for excellence not as burdens but as cherished memories tied to fun, friendship, and connection. From this story, Linsin draws a broader lesson: when a classroom is genuinely enjoyable and filled with a spirit of fun and humor, teachers can ask a great deal of their students — more independent work, stricter routines, higher standards — without students resenting it. The affection students feel for a class experience they love makes them willing to meet even very high expectations. Linsin frames this as evidence that ambition and enjoyment are not in tension but reinforce one another.
points: Students who experience a classroom as genuinely enjoyable will look back fondly on hard work and high expectations rather than resent them.
A spirit of fun and humor in the classroom fabric enables teachers to ask more of students without pushback.
High expectations paired with genuine care and enjoyment build lasting, positive connections with former students.
Rigorous work habits and demanding routines can coexist with — and even be remembered as part of — a beloved classroom experience.
As long as students feel a class is worth their while, they will follow a teacher's high expectations willingly.
quotes: I’ve since learned that as long as you create a classroom your students look forward to, you can’t ask for too much. You can’t have expectations that are too high.
Your students will rise to meet your high bar as long as they know you care enough to make it worth their while.
As long as you make your classroom an experience they enjoy being part of—better yet, love being part of—they will follow you to the ends of the earth.
He never mentioned the lengthy independent work periods, the demand for flawless routines, or my neverending calls for excellence.
Because when a spirit of fun and humor are part of the fabric of your classroom, you can ask for more and for better every day of the week.
